transcripts.title: One Breath Reset
transcripts.transcriptText:
Take one moment to pause.

You do not need to fix anything right now.

Notice that you are already breathing. Let the next breath come in a little slower, and let it leave a little more gently.

Feel one place where your body is supported. Your feet. Your hands. Your back. Wherever support is easiest to notice.

Now let your attention widen. There may be sound. There may be thought. There may be tension. And there is also this breath.

That is enough for this moment.
transcripts.productionNotes: Leave 300-500 ms after the opening line and at the end.

transcripts.title: Name It and Widen
transcripts.transcriptText:
If tinnitus has moved into the center of attention, start by naming it gently.

Ringing.

Buzzing.

Tone.

Whatever word fits best, use it without arguing with it.

Now widen the field. Notice one external sound. Notice one physical sensation. Notice the room around you.

Tinnitus may still be here, but it is not the whole room. It is one part of awareness, alongside everything else your mind can notice.

Let that be the practice.
transcripts.productionNotes: Short pauses after each label word.

transcripts.title: 3-2-1 Senses Mini
transcripts.transcriptText:
Look around and name three things you can see.

One.

Two.

Three.

Now notice two things you can feel. Maybe your clothing against your skin, your feet on the floor, or your hands resting where they are.

Now notice one sound in the space around you.

Take a breath and let these details remind your attention that this moment is bigger than one thought, one feeling, or one sound.

You are here. And there is more here than the mind first noticed.
transcripts.productionNotes: Pause briefly after the count words. This can be paced a little slower than normal speech.

transcripts.title: Sound Therapy Mindful Start
transcripts.transcriptText:
As the sound begins, notice that it does not need to cover everything.

Let it be a steady backdrop.

Notice the support sound. Notice your body. Notice the space you are in.

If tinnitus is present, you do not have to push it away. Let the support sound and tinnitus both be part of the listening field.

The goal is not to win a battle with sound. The goal is to give your attention more than one place to rest.
transcripts.productionNotes: Good with a very soft sound bed, but render voice dry for app flexibility.

transcripts.title: Three-Minute Breathing Space for Tinnitus
transcripts.transcriptText:
Begin by taking a comfortable position. You can sit, stand, or lie down.

Let your eyes close if that feels okay. If not, soften your gaze.

First, notice what is here.

There may be tinnitus. There may be thoughts about tinnitus. There may be emotion in the body, or tension in the face, shoulders, chest, or stomach.

You do not need to change any of it yet. Just notice what has arrived.

Now bring attention to the breath.

You do not need to breathe perfectly. Feel the next inhale. Feel the next exhale. Let the breath be an anchor, not a test.

If your attention goes back to tinnitus, that is not failure. It is simply the next moment to return to the breath.

Now widen awareness.

Include the breath. Include the body. Include sounds in the room. If tinnitus is present, include that too.

Let tinnitus be one part of the field, not the whole field.

For the next few breaths, practice staying with the whole moment.

Breath. Body. Sound. Space.

When you are ready, open your eyes or lift your gaze.

Choose one next action that supports you. It can be small. Turn on a comfortable sound. Continue your activity. Stretch. Drink water. Or simply move into the next moment with a little more steadiness.
transcripts.productionNotes: Add 2-3 second pauses between the three phases: notice, breathe, widen.

transcripts.title: Body Anchor and Room Sounds
transcripts.transcriptText:
Find a position that feels steady enough for the next few minutes.

Begin with the body.

Notice where your body meets support. Your feet on the floor. Your legs against the chair. Your back, your hands, or the weight of your body resting.

You do not need to relax on command. Just notice support.

Now shift attention to sounds around you.

Maybe there is a fan, traffic, a voice in the distance, a hum, or the soft sound of your own breathing.

Listen without needing to name everything. Let the sounds come and go.

Now bring body and sound together.

Feel support beneath you, and hear the space around you.

If a thought interrupts, let it be a thought. If a feeling interrupts, let it be a feeling. You can notice it and return to body and sound.

For a few breaths, rest attention in this larger field.

Body supported.

Sounds arriving and fading.

Breath moving on its own.

Before finishing, notice whether anything shifted. It does not need to be dramatic. Maybe you feel calmer. Maybe you simply feel more aware.

Either way, you practiced returning to the present moment.
transcripts.productionNotes: Good medium practice. Avoid overly sleepy pacing unless intended.

transcripts.title: Sound Shifting Short Practice
transcripts.transcriptText:
Begin by choosing a comfortable posture.

If you have a gentle sound in the room, such as a fan, rain sound, or soft music, let it play at a comfortable level. If not, use whatever sound is already present.

Start by noticing the body.

Feel one point of contact. Feet. Seat. Hands. Back.

Now gently notice tinnitus, if it is present.

You are not trying to like it. You are not trying to make it louder. You are simply noticing: there is the sound.

After a few seconds, shift attention to an external sound.

Listen to the fan, the room, traffic, music, or any sound outside the tinnitus.

Now shift to the body again.

Feel the breath. Feel your hands. Feel the support beneath you.

Now gently return to tinnitus for just a moment.

Notice whether the mind reacts. If it does, silently label the reaction: thought, feeling, frustration, fear, or memory.

Now shift back to the external sound.

Let your attention move on purpose.

Tinnitus.

External sound.

Body.

Room.

You are practicing flexibility. You do not need tinnitus to vanish in order to move your attention.

Before finishing, take one slow breath.

Notice that attention can move. That is the skill.
transcripts.productionNotes: Use slow pacing with short pauses after 'Tinnitus. External sound. Body. Room.'

transcripts.title: Open Hands Grounding
transcripts.transcriptText:
Let your hands rest somewhere comfortable.

You can place them on your lap, on the arms of a chair, or gently against each other.

Bring attention to the hands.

Notice temperature. Warm, cool, neutral.

Notice pressure. Notice contact. Notice any pulsing, tingling, dryness, or movement.

If you do not notice much, that is okay. Noticing little is still noticing.

Now slowly open the hands.

Let the fingers soften.

Notice the difference between holding and releasing.

On the next breath in, feel the hands.

On the breath out, let the hands soften again.

You might imagine that the hands are showing the rest of the body how to loosen its grip.

Not forced. Not dramatic. Just a little less holding.

If the mind wanders, return to the hands.

At the end, gently move the fingers.

Carry that small release into the next thing you do.
transcripts.productionNotes: Can be rendered with a slightly intimate, quiet tone.

transcripts.title: Settling Without Forcing Sleep
transcripts.transcriptText:
Let this be a transition, not a test.

You do not have to force sleep.

If you are lying down, feel the bed supporting you. If you are sitting, feel the chair, the floor, or the surface beneath your body.

Let the eyes close or soften.

Notice the breath as it is.

There is no perfect way to breathe at bedtime. There is only this breath, and then the next one.

If tinnitus is present, notice how quickly the mind may want to solve it, measure it, or predict the night.

For now, let the job be simpler.

Notice the body.

Notice the breath.

Notice the space around you.

If sound therapy is playing, let it be a soft background, not something you have to monitor.

If thoughts about sleep appear, try saying: this is a difficult moment, and I do not need to solve the whole night right now.

Let the next exhale be a small permission to stop working so hard.

The body knows more about sleep than the thinking mind does.

You can give it a quieter place to begin.

Rest here for a few breaths.

Nothing to force.

Nothing to prove.

Just settling.
transcripts.productionNotes: Should be slow, warm, with modest pauses. Avoid saying 'you will sleep'.

transcripts.title: Mindful Listening with Tinnitus and External Sound
transcripts.displayTitle: Mindful Listening with Tinnitus and External Sound
transcripts.sourceTitle: Mindful Listening with Tinnitus and External Sound
transcripts.transcriptText:
Find a comfortable position and let your attention settle.

You may want a gentle sound in the background. A fan, soft rain, quiet nature sound, or another sound that feels easy to hear.

Begin by noticing the body.

Feel where you are supported. Let the shoulders drop by even a small amount. Let the jaw soften if it wants to.

Now listen.

Do not search for anything yet. Let the sounds come to you.

There may be sound in the room. There may be sound outside the room. There may be the sound of your breath, your clothing, the chair, or a soft hum in the environment.

There may also be tinnitus.

If tinnitus is present, notice how the mind relates to it.

Does it tighten? Does it judge? Does it start a story?

You do not need to stop that reaction. Just notice it.

Now gently label the tinnitus with a neutral word.

Ringing.

Tone.

Buzzing.

Sound.

Use whatever word fits without adding an argument.

After labeling it, widen attention again.

Listen for one sound outside the tinnitus.

Now feel one sensation in the body.

Now notice the space around you.

Let the listening field become wider.

Tinnitus may remain part of it. That is okay.

The practice is not to force tinnitus out. The practice is to notice that it can be present without being the only thing you hear.

For the next few moments, move attention gently.

External sound.

Body.

Room.

Tinnitus, if present.

External sound again.

If frustration appears, label it gently: frustration.

If fear appears, label it gently: fear.

If the mind says, I do not want this, label that as thought.

Then return to listening.

You are not trying to win against sound.

You are practicing a different relationship with sound.

Let the support sound be simple.

Let your breath be simple.

Let attention widen again.

Now notice whether tinnitus feels exactly the same, or whether your relationship to it has shifted even slightly.

Maybe it is still there, but less central.

Maybe it is still central, but you found one moment of space around it.

Either way, the practice counts.

Before finishing, take one slow breath in.

Let it out gently.

Choose one sound, one body sensation, or one object in the room to carry forward as your anchor.

When you are ready, open your eyes or lift your gaze.

The goal was not to erase tinnitus. The goal was to remember that awareness can hold more than one sound.
transcripts.productionNotes: Use pauses between attention shifts. Good candidate for mild sound bed under voice if desired.

transcripts.title: Short Full-Body Scan
transcripts.transcriptText:
Find a position that lets the body be supported.

You can lie down, sit back, or rest in any posture that feels safe and steady.

Let the eyes close, or soften your gaze.

Start with the breath.

There is no need to change it. Just notice that breathing is happening.

Now bring attention to the feet.

Notice the toes, the soles, the heels, and the contact with the surface beneath you.

If there is sensation, notice it. If there is little sensation, notice that too.

Move attention to the ankles and lower legs.

Feel the calves, shins, and knees.

Notice whether these areas feel heavy, light, tense, relaxed, warm, cool, or neutral.

There is no need to make them different.

Now move to the thighs and hips.

Feel the weight of the legs. Feel the contact and support beneath you.

With the next exhale, allow the lower body to be just as it is.

Bring attention to the pelvis and lower back.

Notice any tightness or pressure. Notice any softness or ease.

Let the breath move naturally.

Now shift attention to the belly.

Feel the belly rise and fall, or simply notice the movement of breathing somewhere in the body.

Move to the chest and upper back.

Notice expansion. Notice stillness. Notice the places that move and the places that do not.

Now bring attention to the shoulders.

Many people hold effort here.

You do not have to force the shoulders down. Just notice them.

If they soften, let them soften. If they do not, let that be okay.

Move down the arms.

Upper arms. Elbows. Forearms. Wrists. Palms. Fingers.

Notice the hands as a whole.

Now bring awareness to the throat and neck.

Notice swallowing, breathing, tightness, or space.

Move to the jaw.

If the teeth are pressed together, you can let the jaw loosen slightly.

Bring attention to the mouth, cheeks, eyes, forehead, and scalp.

Let the face be held by awareness without needing to arrange it.

Now feel the whole body.

Feet and legs.

Belly and chest.

Arms and hands.

Neck and face.

The whole body breathing.

If the mind wanders, that is part of practice. Gently return to the body as a whole.

Rest here for a few breaths.

Supported.

Breathing.

Aware.

When you are ready, begin to notice the room again.

Move the fingers or toes.

Open the eyes or lift the gaze.

Take this steadiness with you, even if it is only a small amount.
transcripts.productionNotes: Body scan. Add 3-5 sec pauses between body regions during final production.

transcripts.title: Acceptance in the Present Moment
transcripts.transcriptText:
Begin in a position that feels steady.

Let the body be supported.

Take a breath in, and let the exhale be a little longer than usual.

Now notice what is present.

There may be tinnitus.

There may be thoughts about tinnitus.

There may be a wish that this experience were different.

All of that can be included.

Acceptance does not mean liking tinnitus.

It does not mean giving up.

For this practice, acceptance means telling the truth about this moment, so you can stop spending all of your energy fighting what is already here.

Gently notice the sound, if it is present.

You do not have to move toward it aggressively. You do not have to stare at it with your attention.

Just notice: this is part of the moment.

Now notice the body.

Maybe there is tension. Maybe the shoulders or jaw are holding effort.

Let the body be part of the moment too.

Now notice one external sound.

Let tinnitus and external sound both exist in the same field.

Now notice one place where the body is supported.

Let sound and support both exist.

If the mind says, I cannot accept this, notice that too.

That is a thought.

A very understandable thought.

You might try saying quietly: I do not have to like this, and I can still take care of myself.

Let that sentence settle.

I do not have to like this, and I can still take care of myself.

Now widen attention again.

Sound.

Body.

Breath.

Room.

Support.

This moment may not be the moment you would choose.

But it is the moment you can work with.

From here, one useful action becomes possible.

Maybe that action is turning on comfortable sound.

Maybe it is returning to what you were doing.

Maybe it is resting.

Maybe it is asking for support.

For the next few breaths, let the practice be simple.

Notice what is here.

Soften the struggle by one degree.

Choose one next useful step.

Before finishing, place attention on the body again.

Feel the surface beneath you.

Take one steady breath.

When you are ready, open your eyes or lift your gaze.

Acceptance is not the end of change.

It is often where change can begin.
transcripts.productionNotes: Use calm, deliberate pacing. Good after Acceptance chapter.

transcripts.title: Evening Body and Sound Wind-Down
transcripts.transcriptText:
Let this be a wind-down, not a performance.

You do not have to make sleep happen during this practice.

You are only creating conditions that let the body move toward rest.

Find a position that feels comfortable enough.

If you are lying down, feel the bed beneath you. If you are sitting, feel the support beneath your body.

Let the eyes close or soften.

Start by noticing the breath.

Do not control it yet. Just notice the rhythm.

If tinnitus is present, let it be part of the room of awareness.

If a gentle background sound is playing, let it remain soft.

Now bring attention to the face.

Let the forehead smooth.

Let the eyes rest.

Let the jaw loosen by a small amount.

Move attention to the shoulders.

As you exhale, let the shoulders become heavier.

Move to the arms and hands.

Notice any warmth, coolness, tingling, or stillness.

Let the hands rest.

Now bring attention to the chest and belly.

The body may still feel alert.

That is okay.

Instead of demanding sleep, offer steadiness.

Inhale gently.

Exhale slowly.

Now notice the sounds around you.

The room may be quiet, or not quiet.

There may be tinnitus.

There may be sound therapy.

There may be distant sound.

Let the sounds be present without needing to follow each one.

If the mind starts measuring the night, notice that.

Thought.

Planning.

Worry.

Then return to the body.

The body supported.

The breath moving.

The sounds present.

Now move attention to the legs.

Thighs. Knees. Calves. Ankles. Feet.

Let the lower body be heavy.

Let the surface beneath you do some of the work.

If a sleep thought appears, such as, I need to fall asleep now, try softening it.

Maybe: I am resting, and rest still matters.

Or: I do not have to solve the whole night right now.

Let that be enough.

Now feel the whole body.

Face soft.

Shoulders heavy.

Hands resting.

Belly moving.

Legs supported.

Sounds present.

Breath steady.

Nothing to force.

Nothing to prove.

If sleep comes, let it come.

If sleep does not come right away, you are still practicing a calmer relationship with the night.

Stay here for a few more breaths.

When you are ready, either let the practice fade into rest, or gently return to the room and decide your next supportive step.
transcripts.productionNotes: Longer pauses can make this 8-10 min. Should be slow, bedtime tone.

transcripts.title: Full Body Scan with Tinnitus as One Part of Awareness
transcripts.sourceTitle: Full Body Scan with Tinnitus as One Part of Awareness
transcripts.transcriptText:
Find a comfortable position where your body can be supported for a while.

You may lie on your back, sit in a supportive chair, or choose any position that feels safe and sustainable.

Let your hands rest in a natural place.

Let your feet fall however they want to fall.

If closing your eyes feels comfortable, close them. If not, soften your gaze and let the room be unfocused.

Begin by noticing that the body is already here.

There is nothing you need to perform.

There is no perfect mindfulness state to reach.

For the next while, the practice is to move attention through the body, notice what is present, and return gently when the mind wanders.

Start with the breath.

Feel the inhale.

Feel the exhale.

If the breath is shallow, let it be shallow.

If the breath is deep, let it be deep.

Now notice the places where the body is supported.

The back. The legs. The feet. The arms. Wherever contact is easiest to feel.

Let the body receive that support.

Now bring attention to the toes of the left foot.

Notice any sensation there.

Warmth. Coolness. Tingling. Pressure. Numbness. Or no clear sensation.

All of those are acceptable.

Move attention to the sole of the left foot.

Feel the heel.

Feel the arch.

Feel the top of the foot.

Let attention rest there for a few breaths.

Now move to the left ankle.

Notice the ankle as a joint, a place of movement and support.

Move to the lower left leg.

Calf and shin.

Notice any tightness, heaviness, pulsing, or stillness.

You do not need to change it.

With the next exhale, let the leg be held by the surface beneath you.

Now bring attention to the left knee.

The front of the knee.

The back of the knee.

The space inside and around the joint.

Now the left thigh.

Notice the weight of the thigh.

Notice contact.

Notice any effort the leg may still be holding.

If it softens, let it soften.

If it does not, simply notice.

Move attention to the left hip.

Feel where the leg meets the pelvis.

Now sense the whole left leg.

Toes.

Foot.

Ankle.

Lower leg.

Knee.

Thigh.

Hip.

Let the whole left leg rest.

Now shift attention to the toes of the right foot.

Again, notice what is present without needing a particular sensation.

Move to the sole of the right foot.

Heel. Arch. Top of the foot.

Feel the foot as a whole.

Now the right ankle.

The lower right leg.

Calf and shin.

Let attention move slowly enough that the body has time to be noticed.

Now the right knee.

The right thigh.

The right hip.

Notice whether the two legs feel the same or different.

There is no problem to solve.

Now feel both legs together.

Heavy or light.

Tense or relaxed.

Clear or unclear.

Both legs included in awareness.

Bring attention to the pelvis.

Notice the contact with the surface beneath you.

Feel the hips.

Feel the lower belly.

Feel the lower back.

This area may hold tension, discomfort, or stillness.

Let the breath move through the body naturally.

Now bring attention to the belly.

Feel the belly rise and fall, if that movement is available.

If it is not, notice any other part of the breath.

The chest.

The ribs.

The nostrils.

Let the breath be known.

Move awareness to the lower back.

Then the middle back.

Then the upper back.

Notice the length of the spine.

Notice where the back meets support.

With each exhale, allow the back to release one small layer of effort if it wants to.

Now bring attention to the chest.

Feel the chest rise and fall.

Feel the ribs moving.

Notice the area around the heart.

There may be emotion here.

If emotion is present, include it gently.

Mindfulness is not pushing away.

Mindfulness is making space to notice.

Now bring attention to the shoulders.

The left shoulder.

The right shoulder.

The space across the upper back.

Many people hold the day here.

You do not have to force the shoulders to relax.

Just let them be noticed.

Now move attention down the left arm.

Upper arm.

Elbow.

Forearm.

Wrist.

Palm.

Fingers.

Notice the whole left hand.

Now the right arm.

Upper arm.

Elbow.

Forearm.

Wrist.

Palm.

Fingers.

Notice the whole right hand.

Now feel both arms and hands together.

Resting.

Supported.

Included.

Now bring attention to the neck and throat.

Notice the front of the throat.

The sides of the neck.

The back of the neck.

Let the head be supported as much as possible.

Bring attention to the jaw.

If the jaw is clenched, see if it can soften slightly.

Let the tongue rest.

Let the lips soften.

Bring attention to the cheeks.

The nose.

The eyes.

Let the area around the eyes be soft.

Now the forehead.

The scalp.

The top of the head.

Feel the whole head resting in awareness.

At this point, if tinnitus is present, notice it gently.

Not as the enemy of the practice.

Not as proof that the practice is failing.

Simply as one sound experience that may be present.

Let tinnitus be included alongside the body.

The feet.

The legs.

The belly.

The chest.

The hands.

The face.

The breath.

The room.

Tinnitus can be one part of the whole field, not the whole field itself.

If the mind reacts, label the reaction softly.

Thought.

Feeling.

Judgment.

Memory.

Worry.

Then return to the body as a whole.

Now sense the whole body breathing.

From the toes to the top of the head.

From the top of the head to the toes.

The whole body supported.

The whole body present.

Nothing to force.

Nothing to prove.

For a few breaths, rest in this wider awareness.

If tinnitus is present, let it float within the larger field.

If it is not noticeable, that is okay too.

The goal is not to make anything happen.

The goal is to practice being with experience without being pulled entirely into one part of it.

Now begin to bring awareness back to the room.

Notice the surface beneath you.

Notice the air around you.

Notice any external sounds.

Take a slightly deeper breath.

Move the fingers.

Move the toes.

If the eyes are closed, open them slowly.

Before you move on, notice one word that describes how you feel now.

Calm.

Heavy.

Settled.

Tired.

Aware.

Whatever word appears is fine.

Carry that awareness into the next part of your day.
transcripts.productionNotes: To reach 18-22 min, add 5-15 sec silent pauses between body regions and 30-45 sec resting periods after whole-body awareness paragraphs. No pause tags in clean text.
